analysis.investment_thesis: Eureka Forbes owns India's most trusted water purifier brand (Aquaguard) with a massive direct-to-home service network — a genuine moat — but at 47x earnings for only ~11% revenue growth, the story doesn't justify the price. The PEG of ~2.4x (P/E 47 ÷ sustainable ~20% earnings growth) screams overvalued; I'd want to see this closer to INR 280–300 before getting excited.
key_strengths: Brand moat: Aquaguard is synonymous with water purifiers in India — every household knows it, giving pricing power and AMC (Annual Maintenance Contract) recurring revenue
Clean balance sheet: D/E of just 0.02 with INR 96 Cr cash and rapidly declining debt (from INR 256 Cr in 2022 to INR 26 Cr in 2025)
Improving FCF: Free cash flow grew from INR 167 Cr → 169 Cr → 190 Cr over FY23-25, demonstrating the capital-light nature of the service model
key_risks: Terrible ROE of 3.71% — INR 4,520 Cr of equity generating only INR 164 Cr profit signals massive goodwill/intangibles from the 2022 restructuring that dilutes returns permanently
Revenue growth is modest at ~11% (FY24→FY25: INR 2,189 Cr → 2,437 Cr) — nowhere near the 20%+ I need to justify a 47x P/E multiple
Operating margins at 7.97% are thin for a premium consumer brand — competition from Kent, Livpure, and Xiaomi is real, and margins should be 12–15% for a company of this brand strength
red_flags: PEG ratio ~2.4x far exceeds my 1.0 threshold — you're overpaying significantly for the growth on offer
Investing CF spiked to -INR 168 Cr in FY25 vs. -INR 32 Cr in FY24 — what are they acquiring or spending on? Story needs clarity
ROE 3.71% is below cost of capital — this business is not yet earning its keep on the equity base inherited from the restructuring
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Eureka Forbes is a classic Lynch "invest in what you know" brand — Aquaguard has been in Indian homes for 40 years, and the direct-to-home sales force plus AMC subscription model creates genuine switching costs. The underlying business is genuinely improving: net profit surged from INR 26 Cr (FY23) → INR 96 Cr (FY24) → INR 164 Cr (FY25), and OCF is tracking ahead of net income, which is a healthy sign. But the problem is simple arithmetic: at INR 482, you're paying 47x earnings for a company growing revenues at ~11% and operating margins of only 7.97%. This is not a fast grower — it's a stalwart at best.

The elephant in the room is the balance sheet: INR 4,520 Cr of equity generating INR 164 Cr in profit gives an ROE of 3.71% — that's roughly half what a fixed deposit pays. The 2022 restructuring loaded up the balance sheet with goodwill that will suppress ROE for years. For Lynch, a business needs to earn at least 12% ROE to compound wealth. Until earnings scale to INR 350–400 Cr (which could take 3–4 years at current trajectory), the valuation is simply too full. I'd revisit at forward P/E of 20–22x or if management demonstrates a credible path to 12%+ operating margins.
